area: Area IV. Takeoffs, Landings, and Go-Arounds
objective: By the end of this lesson you can decide early and on purpose to reject a landing, fly the go-around in power, attitude, configuration order (including flaps-then-gear cleanup in a complex airplane), hold VX or VY within commercial tolerances (plus or minus 5 knots), and manage traffic, wake, wind, LAHSO and ATC along the way.
why: The go-around is a normal maneuver that only turns dangerous when it is delayed or flown badly, and the most critical one starts close to the ground [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Many power-on stall/spin accidents have happened during go-arounds, often from a nose-high trim setting or flaps raised too early [[13:11|AC 61-67C para 104]]. A commercial pilot is expected to make that call without hesitation and fly it precisely, in any airplane.

warmup: Think first: you are 20 ft above the runway with full flaps, trimmed nose-up, slow, and a deer runs onto the runway. You shove the throttle forward. What will the airplane do in the next three seconds if you do nothing else, and which of your next moves could hurt you most?

The belief that conditions are not as bad as they are and the approach is sure to end safely. One of the two usual causes of a late go-around [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
A constant-angle glide path toward a chosen point, at a constant final descent airspeed and configuration [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].
Altitude and speed are both off in the same direction (lower and slower, or higher and faster). Fix it with the throttle [[24:98|AFH 4-12]].
Altitude and speed are off in opposite directions (higher and slower, or lower and faster). Fix it with the elevator, trading one for the other [[24:98|AFH 4-12]].
Best angle of climb speed: the most altitude gain for a given distance over the ground. Used to clear obstacles [[24:78|AFH 3-17]].
Best rate of climb speed: the most altitude gain in a given time [[24:78|AFH 3-17]].
Feet of altitude gained per 100 ft of horizontal travel, in percent. Unlike rate of climb, it is changed by wind [[24:259|AFH 13-10]].
Less induced drag near the surface, felt up to about one wingspan high. Its extra performance is 'borrowed' and paid back as you climb out [[24:142|AFH 6-10]] [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].
A quick trim change, right after setting the climb attitude, to take off the heavy control pressure; fine trim comes later [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
VLO is the highest speed for moving the gear through its cycle; VLE is the highest speed with the gear down. Both are in the AFM/POH and often on a placard [[24:247|AFH 12-16]].
Any aircraft, vehicle, person or object on the ground that creates a collision hazard or loss of separation with an aircraft taking off or landing [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].

body.p: A go-around is used when approach and landing parameters drift from what you expected or when it is hazardous to continue. ATC requests, a hazard on the runway, overtaking another airplane, wind shear, wake turbulence, a mechanical failure and an unstable approach are all reasons to break off [[24:181|AFH 9-10]]. The idea that a go-around always means a poor approach or a weak pilot is, in the AFH's word, a fallacy [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
The maneuver has three cardinal principles, in this order: power, attitude, configuration [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. The figure shows the whole picture, from the decision to the cruise climb.

body.p: So the commercial checkride does not add new steps. It takes away the fast-side cushion on your climb speed and adds an oral element: you must explain the procedure, why timing matters and which airspeeds to fly. In some airplanes a 5-knot error from the recommended speed can significantly reduce climb performance [[24:142|AFH 6-10]], so the tight band matters.

callout.text: The AFM/POH procedure for your airplane comes first. If the AFH differs from the manufacturer's recommendations, the manufacturer's recommendations take precedence [[24:172|AFH 9-1]]. The ACS lets you configure 'after a positive rate of climb has been verified or in accordance with airplane manufacturer's instructions' (ACS CA.IV.N.S5).
Power, attitude, configuration. Say it out loud as you push the throttle.

check.q: Which two ACS skill tolerances are tighter for the commercial go-around than for the private?
check.a: The climb speed after applying power (VX or VY ±5 knots instead of +10/-5) and VY to a safe maneuvering altitude (±5 knots instead of +10/-5) (ACS CA.IV.N.S4, S7; PA.IV.N.S4, S7).

body.p: Most go-around decisions are made on final, so the first defense is knowing what 'stabilized' means. Typically you go around if not stabilized by 500 ft above airport elevation in VMC or 1,000 ft in IMC. In a typical piston airplane in the traffic pattern, go around immediately if the approach becomes unstabilized below 300 ft AGL [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

body.p: Energy management is the skill behind those numbers. Altitude and airspeed are the two places your energy lives. If both are off in the same direction (lower and slower, higher and faster), that is a total energy error, fixed with the throttle. If they are off in opposite directions, that is a distribution error, fixed with the elevator. A mix of both needs both controls at once [[24:98|AFH 4-12]].

The far-left column of the chart is the one that matters for go-arounds. If you have slowed far enough, even full throttle may give no surplus energy. Then the only way out is to push forward first, lowering the angle of attack and induced drag, and only then gain energy with power. Too close to the ground, there may not be enough room to do that [[24:99|AFH 4-13]].

callout.text: Retracting flaps to fix an undershoot can cause a sudden loss of lift and a high sink rate [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. Unstable, slow approaches and high-drag go-arounds where the gear or flaps are left down are named examples of running out of energy at low altitude [[24:103|AFH 4-17]].

check.q: You are below the glide path and 10 knots fast. Is that a total energy error or a distribution error, and which control fixes it?
check.a: A distribution error (lower and faster). Pull back on the elevator to climb and slow at the same time, keeping the throttle where it is (box 9 in Figure 4-12) [[24:99|AFH 4-13]].

chunks.title: When to decide, and why pilots wait

body.p: A go-around is not dangerous in itself. It becomes dangerous only when delayed unduly or flown improperly, and the most critical one is started very close to the ground [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Delay normally comes from two sources: landing expectancy (the belief that it will work out) and pride (the belief that going around admits failure) [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

The FAA's general aviation safety guidance asks instructors to teach pilots to reject an approach and go around when they cannot maintain a stabilized approach, and to make stabilized approaches a standard practice [[15:11|AC 61-98E 2.1.3.4]]. In plain words: decide what 'unsafe' looks like before you are in it.

body.p: Notice the pattern: almost every trigger gets worse the lower and slower you are, and the go-around itself also gets harder as you get lower and slower. That is the real meaning of 'timely' in ACS CA.IV.N.S3. A go-around from 300 ft with normal speed is easy; the same decision made at 10 ft with the speed decaying is the most critical one there is [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

callout.text: Commercial habit: brief your personal triggers on downwind. For example: 'Not stable by 500, go around. Unstable below 300, go around. Not down in the first third, go around.' The words commit you before landing expectancy can kick in [[24:177|AFH 9-6]] [[24:203|AFH 9-32]].

check.q: Name the two sources of go-around delay and give one practical way to beat each.
check.a: Landing expectancy and pride [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Application: brief fixed triggers before final to beat expectancy, and treat every go-around as a normal maneuver (the AFH calls the 'poor approach' stigma a fallacy) to beat pride [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

chunks.title: Power: full, smooth and right away

body.p: Power is your first concern. The instant you decide, apply full or maximum allowable takeoff power, smoothly and without hesitation, and hold it until flying speed and control are back. A settling airplane has inertia to overcome. Turn carburetor heat off for full power, if applicable [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

bullets: Smooth and positive, not abrupt: in some airplanes an abrupt throttle movement makes the engine falter [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
Constant-speed propeller: maximum takeoff power means the propeller control all the way forward (low pitch, high rpm) and the throttle to the maximum allowable manifold pressure [[24:236|AFH 12-5]].
A rapid throttle push can cause a momentary propeller overspeed, usually not serious if rated rpm is not exceeded by 10 percent for more than 3 seconds [[24:240|AFH 12-9]].

Turbocharged engines: all power control movements should be slow and smooth, because aggressive throttle movements raise the chance of overboosting. Watch the engine gauges as you add power [[24:241|AFH 12-10]].

Full power at high pitch and low speed means strong left-turning tendency from P-factor; not enough rudder leads to uncoordinated flight, which sets up a spin if the critical angle of attack is reached [[13:12|AC 61-67C para 109]].

body.p: Power also moves the nose. More airflow over the tail plus the nose-up trim you set for the approach makes the nose rise sharply and turn left [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]. That is why power and attitude are really one motion: throttle forward with one hand, forward pressure and right rudder with the rest of you.

callout.text: The FAA's experimental-airplane guidance names a possible accident scenario: rapidly applying power in a go-around without controlling the pitch and yaw tendencies [[57:8|AC 90-109A para 6]]. High-power airplanes make this worse.

check.q: In a turbocharged complex single, why should you not slam the throttle forward even in a hurried go-around?
check.a: Aggressive throttle movement raises the chance of overboosting the engine; movements should be slow and smooth while you watch the gauges [[24:241|AFH 12-10]]. Smooth but positive is also the AFH rule for every go-around [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

chunks.title: Attitude and airspeed: VX or VY within 5 knots

body.p: An airplane cannot fly below its stall speed and cannot climb below its minimum power required speed. Resist the urge to pitch up for a climb if the airspeed is not there. Sometimes it is better to lower the nose briefly to gain airspeed and stay off the back side of the power curve [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

With low-speed trim set, the sudden power tends to raise the nose and yaw the airplane left. Letting the nose rise too early at low altitude could cause an unrecoverable stall. Expect to need considerable forward pressure, use right rudder for torque and P-factor, then rough trim once the climb attitude and airspeed are set [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. If the elevator trim stall develops fully, recovery needs a big nose-down attitude and a big altitude loss [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

Which speed? VX gives the most altitude in the shortest horizontal distance and is used to clear obstacles; VY gives the most altitude in the shortest time [[24:78|AFH 3-17]]. VX is usually slightly less than VY [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]. With trees or a tower past the runway end, VX is the 'appropriate' speed of ACS S4; otherwise VY. Either way, the commercial band is ±5 knots, and S7 then asks for VY ±5 knots up to a safe maneuvering altitude (ACS CA.IV.N.S4, S7).

These speeds move with altitude. As altitude increases, VX increases and VY decreases, until they meet at the absolute ceiling. Check the AFM/POH for the right speeds in the conditions you have [[24:78|AFH 3-17]]. Maximum rate of climb may not be enough to clear an obstacle that maximum angle of climb would clear [[1:263|PHAK 11-7]].

callout.text: Low-speed go-arounds, such as from the round out or after a bad bounce: the first priority is control and flying speed, and a few moments of level or nearly level flight may be needed while the airplane accelerates to climb speed. The AFH gives this note in its twin-engine chapter [[24:272|AFH 13-23]]; its single-engine go-around section makes the same point, that it may be better to lower the nose briefly to gain airspeed [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

check.q: POH: VX 63 KIAS, VY 76 KIAS at sea level. You go around at a 4,000 ft airport. Which way do the two speeds move, and what band does the examiner allow?
check.a: VX increases and VY decreases with altitude, so use the POH values for that altitude [[24:78|AFH 3-17]]. Whichever is appropriate, hold it within ±5 knots, then VY ±5 knots to a safe maneuvering altitude (ACS CA.IV.N.S4, S7).

body.p: A go-around close to the ground starts inside ground effect. Pilots are often lulled by the apparent 'cushion of air.' It is imaginary: the extra performance comes from reduced induced drag, it is borrowed, and it is repaid when you climb out. Try to climb too soon and the airplane may not climb, or even hold altitude, at full power [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

head: Fact
Source
rows: Ground effect normally occurs up to about one wingspan above the surface
Induced drag is about 25 percent lower at one-quarter span and about 50 percent lower at one-tenth span
In ground effect, the airspeed indicator and altimeter read slightly low and the VSI usually shows a descent
Climbing out: more angle of attack needed, more induced drag and thrust required, a pitch-up tendency, and the indicated airspeed rises
With high weight, high density altitude and high temperature, an airplane short on airspeed may get airborne in ground effect but be unable to keep flying out of it

body.p: Two commercial-level traps come out of that table. First, your instruments lie a little in ground effect, so a VSI showing a descent is not proof you are sinking. Second, the pitch-up tendency as you leave ground effect adds to the trim and power pitch-up you are already fighting. Hold the attitude, let the speed build, then climb.

callout.text: 'Attempting to climb out of ground effect prematurely' is on the AFH list of common go-around errors [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

check.q: Why might the VSI show a descent right after you add full power just above the runway, even though you are not sinking?
check.a: Ground effect raises local static pressure, which makes the airspeed and altimeter read slightly low and usually makes the VSI show a descent [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

chunks.title: Configuration: flaps, then gear, then the rest

body.p: After climb attitude and power are set, flaps are next. Once the descent has stopped, move the landing flaps partway or to the takeoff setting the manufacturer recommends. Retract them in small steps so the airplane can accelerate as they come up. A sudden, complete retraction can cost so much lift that the airplane settles into the ground [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

Unless the AFM/POH says otherwise, flaps come up (at least partly) before the gear, for two reasons: on most airplanes full flaps make more drag than the gear, and if the airplane touches down by accident early in the go-around, you want the gear down and locked. The gear comes up after a positive rate of climb, only after rough trim, and when it is certain the airplane will stay airborne [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

Why the pitch keeps changing: extended flaps create a nose-down pitching moment that you trimmed out. Full power adds airflow and lift and makes big pitch changes, and the pitch-up does not fully go away as the flaps come up because of the trim setting. Expect quick changes in pitch force as you clean up [[24:235|AFH 12-4]]. Using the same flap settings at the same points in every pattern gives you a familiar, preplanned go-around sequence [[24:236|AFH 12-5]].
Retractable gear details for the complex airplane [[24:247|AFH 12-16]]:

bullets: Do not retract until a positive rate of climb shows on the instruments; without it the airplane may settle back onto the runway with the gear up.
Leaning forward to reach the gear selector can push the yoke forward and make the airplane descend.
As the gear retracts, airspeed rises and the pitch may change; it can take several seconds. Learn the normal sound and feel so you notice an abnormal cycle.
Respect the gear operating speed (VLO). It may not be marked on the airspeed indicator; look in the AFM/POH and on the placard.

body.p: On that placard the gear may be retracted ('GEAR UP') only at or below 107 KIAS, while it may be extended or flown extended up to 129 KIAS [[24:247|AFH 12-16]]. A go-around normally stays far below these speeds, but a long, fast climb-out before cleaning up can catch you.

callout.text: Certification backs up 'get the drag off': a normal category airplane certified to the current Part 23 must show, out of ground effect, a 3 percent climb gradient in a balked landing with the gear extended and flaps in the landing configuration, without undue pilot workload [[60:101|14 CFR 23.2120(c)]]. Application: that is a small margin, and inside ground effect or with sloppy technique you may not get even that.
AC 61-67C names premature flap retraction and a nose-high trim setting as causal factors in go-around stall/spin accidents [[13:11|AC 61-67C para 104]].

check.q: You are in a complex single, 50 ft up, full flaps, gear down, and the VSI and altimeter just started showing a climb. Rough trim is done. What comes next and why in that order?
check.a: Flaps were already moved partway once the descent stopped; now, with a positive rate confirmed and rough trim done, retract the gear, then the remaining flaps in small steps. Flaps first because full flaps cause more drag than the gear and the gear should stay down in case of an accidental touchdown [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]. Follow your POH if it differs (ACS CA.IV.N.S5).

chunks.title: Wind, density altitude and the climb-out

body.p: Thin air reduces three things at once: engine power (less air in), propeller thrust (less efficient in thin air) and wing lift. High elevation, low pressure, high temperature and high humidity all raise density altitude [[1:91|PHAK 4-4]]. Climb performance falls with more weight, more altitude, gear down or flaps down, because each one cuts excess thrust and power [[1:264|PHAK 11-8]]. A go-around on a hot day at a high field with full flaps stacks all of them.

Wind changes the picture over the ground. Rate of climb is altitude per minute and does not care about wind. Climb gradient is altitude per distance and does: a headwind improves it and a tailwind reduces it [[24:259|AFH 13-10]]. The AFH gives this in its twin-engine chapter, but it is simple geometry for any airplane. A go-around with a tailwind (for example, after a downwind landing attempt) gives a flatter path over the obstacles.

Crosswind correction on the climb-out: once airborne, turn the nose into the wind (crab) with the wings level so you stay over the runway and its extended centerline. Crosswind can change a lot within a few hundred feet of the ground, so check the ground track often and adjust the wind correction angle [[24:140|AFH 6-8]]. That is ACS CA.IV.N.S8.

Wind shear is one of the listed reasons to go around [[24:181|AFH 9-10]]. Be alert for microburst signs early on the approach and ready to go around at the first one; some microbursts cannot be escaped at low altitude [[28:266|AWH 22-11]]. In an encounter, do not let pitch fall below the normal range, and accept lower airspeed to save the flight path [[28:268|AWH 22-13]].

callout.text: Before any landing at a hot, high field, look up the POH balked landing or go-around climb data and VX and VY for that altitude. Know the number before you need it.

check.q: You go around with a 15-knot tailwind instead of a 15-knot headwind, same airspeed and power. What changes: rate of climb, climb gradient, or both?
check.a: Only the climb gradient over the ground; it is reduced by a tailwind and improved by a headwind, while rate of climb is not affected by wind [[24:259|AFH 13-10]].

body.p: Aircraft on final or landing have the right-of-way, but they may not use it to force off a runway an aircraft that has landed and is trying to clear. When two are approaching to land, the lower one has the right-of-way but may not cut in front of or overtake the other [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(g)]]. If the turn to final would create a collision hazard, go around. If traffic on the runway may not clear in time, an early go-around may be in order; go around and inform the controller [[24:168|AFH 8-4]].
Where to fly. ACS S6 asks you to maneuver to the side of the runway when necessary to clear and avoid conflicting traffic (ACS CA.IV.N.S6). The sources describe it this way:

bullets: The upwind leg is a course flown parallel to the landing runway, and it is flown after go-arounds [[24:168|AFH 8-4]].

If the go-around was for conflicting traffic on the ground or aloft, consider maneuvering to the side to keep the traffic in sight, which may be a slight turn to offset from the runway. The AFH says this in its twin-engine chapter, but nothing in it depends on having two engines [[24:272|AFH 13-23]].
At a non-towered airport, airplanes going around should continue straight ahead until beyond the departure end of the runway, watching for traffic established in the pattern [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.6]].
A planned low approach is made straight ahead, with no turns or climb until you have made a thorough visual check for other aircraft, unless ATC authorizes otherwise [[33:256|AIM 4-3-12]].

At a towered airport, unless ATC says otherwise, a VFR go-around overflies the runway while climbing to pattern altitude and enters the pattern on the crosswind leg [[34:353|AIM P/CG]]. Application: a small offset to keep traffic in sight fits inside that, and any ATC instruction comes first [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(b)]].

body.p: Put together (application): offset slightly so the traffic stays out of your blind spot, usually just to the side of the runway, then fly parallel to it and keep going straight past the departure end. Do not climb directly over a departing airplane you cannot see under the nose, and do not turn across the pattern early.

Wake: going around often puts you behind a departing or missed-approach aircraft. Departing behind a larger aircraft, climb above its climb path until turning clear of its wake, and avoid headings that cross below and behind it [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]. After a larger aircraft's low approach, missed approach or touch-and-go, vortices can sit along the runway, so allow at least 2 minutes before your takeoff or landing [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

callout.text: Whether or not the tower gives a wake turbulence caution, you are expected to adjust your flight path to avoid serious wake encounters [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

check.q: You go around because an airplane is still on the runway at a non-towered field. Where do you fly?
check.a: Offset slightly to the side to keep it in sight, flying parallel to the runway [[24:168|AFH 8-4]] [[24:272|AFH 13-23]], then continue straight ahead until beyond the departure end while watching pattern traffic [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.6]].

chunks.title: Radios, ATC, LAHSO and the checklist

body.p: Towered airports. 'Go around' is an ATC instruction to abandon the approach; more instructions may follow. Unless ATC says otherwise, a VFR aircraft overflies the runway while climbing to pattern altitude and enters the pattern on the crosswind leg [[34:353|AIM P/CG]]. Except in an emergency, you may not operate contrary to an ATC instruction where ATC is exercised [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(b)]]. If you go around on your own, tell the controller [[24:168|AFH 8-4]].

bullets: No landing clearance yet on final: ask the tower if you are cleared to land; if there is no response, go around [[7:18|AC 91-73B App 3]].
No radio: a steady red light in flight means give way and continue circling; flashing red means the airport is unsafe, do not land [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]].
Planning a low approach in a Class B, C or D surface area: get tower approval before starting the final approach [[33:256|AIM 4-3-12]].

IFR visual approach: there is no missed approach segment. The tower issues an instruction, and you are responsible for terrain and obstruction avoidance until reaching any assigned altitude [[33:457|AIM 5-4-23]] [[33:458|AIM 5-4-23]].

body.p: Non-towered airports. Self-announce your position and intentions on the CTAF and keep looking; everyone has the see-and-avoid duty [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.2]]. The AC's one sample of a broken-off approach call names the aircraft, where it is and which way it is turning, so other pilots can picture it [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.4.3]].

LAHSO. Accept only if you can land and stop within the Available Landing Distance; you have final authority and should decline if it would compromise safety [[33:253|AIM 4-3-11]] [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]]. Plan it before the flight: know the ALD and slope for each LAHSO combination at your destination and whether your airplane fits [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]]. Once accepted, it is a clearance like any other, but it does not prevent a rejected landing. If you go around, keep safe separation from other aircraft and vehicles and notify the controller promptly [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]]. The crossing traffic you were holding short for is the traffic you now must avoid.

callout.text: Checklist (S1): if you come back to land, re-accomplish the entire before-landing checklist. An interruption of habit like a go-around is a classic setup for a gear-up landing [[24:272|AFH 13-23]]. Retractable airplanes require deliberate, careful, continued checklist use, done on the downwind leg [[24:248|AFH 12-17]].

check.q: You accepted 'cleared to land runway 27, hold short of runway 33' and then balloon badly. May you go around, and what must you do?
check.a: Yes; LAHSO does not preclude a rejected landing. Keep safe separation from other aircraft and vehicles (especially the runway 33 traffic) and notify the controller promptly [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]].

chunks.title: Runway incursions and the wrong surface

body.p: A runway incursion is any occurrence involving an aircraft, vehicle, person or object on the ground that creates a collision hazard or loss of separation with an aircraft taking off or landing [[24:33|AFH 1-12]]. The three major contributing areas are communications, airport knowledge, and flight deck procedures for staying oriented [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].

The data the PHAK gives: about three runway incursions happen each day at towered airports in the United States [[1:365|PHAK 14-31]]; about 65 percent are caused by pilots, and almost half of those by GA pilots. The causal factors are failure to comply with ATC instructions, lack of airport familiarity and not following standard operating procedures [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]].

For the landing pilot, the go-around is the incursion defense. An airplane or vehicle entering your runway, or a takeoff clearance given while you are on short final, is exactly the 'unexpected appearance of hazards on the runway' that calls for a go-around [[24:181|AFH 9-10]]. The earlier you see it, the easier it is, so scan the runway and the hold short lines on final.

bullets: Wrong surface: verify runway alignment and number on every final; if in doubt about the landing surface, go around [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].
Study the airport diagram and lighting before arrival, and use a moving map if you have one [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].
After landing, clear the active runway as soon as possible, then wait for taxi instructions [[1:365|PHAK 14-31]].
Read back all runway hold short instructions verbatim [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]].

callout.text: Runway not clear, landing clearance not heard, surface not certain: any one of these, go around.

check.q: According to the PHAK, roughly what share of runway incursions do pilots cause, and how much of that is GA?
check.a: About 65 percent are caused by pilots, and almost half of those by GA pilots [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]].

chunks.title: Low-altitude traps: stall, spin, CFIT and distraction

body.p: Stalls: many power-on stall/spin accidents happened during go-arounds, with the pilot losing positive control because of a nose-high trim setting or premature flap retraction [[13:11|AC 61-67C para 104]]. The classic P-factor setup is a go-around at high pitch, high power and low airspeed; uncoordinated flight there can turn a stall into a spin [[13:12|AC 61-67C para 109]].

AC 61-67C's go-around stall demonstration shows the two traps. Recover from a full-flap, power-off stall and try to climb with flaps down: a higher than normal pitch can cause a secondary stall, and in some airplanes even a normal climb pitch can. Retract the flaps rapidly while holding a high pitch and you may get a secondary stall or settle with a loss of altitude [[13:17|AC 61-67C para 200f]].
Base-to-final overshoot: the safest action is a go-around. Be reluctant to bank more than 30 degrees that low and never skid the turn to fix it [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

CFIT: controlled flight into terrain is one of the top four causes of fatal GA accidents, and flight at high density altitude and in mountainous terrain are listed contributors [[30:22|RMH 3-4]]. A go-around from a valley or hillside airport may need VX and a planned turn; know the terrain and the climb gradient you need before you start the approach.

Distraction and task saturation: a distraction that pulls your eyes off the instruments or outside is a factor in many accidents, and many begin as a minor problem such as a gauge that reads wrong [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. When overloaded, stop, think, slow down and prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. In a go-around that means flying the airplane first; on airplanes with high control forces at full power, be careful reaching for the flap handle, because control comes first [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

callout.text: Aviate (attitude and airspeed), navigate (where to fly for traffic and terrain), communicate (tower or CTAF). The radio call can wait 10 seconds; the pitch cannot.

check.q: Which two pilot actions does AC 61-67C name as causal factors in go-around stall/spin accidents?
check.a: Failing to keep positive control because of a nose-high trim setting, and premature flap retraction [[13:11|AC 61-67C para 104]].

body.p: The AFH lists these common go-around errors [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]:

bullets: Failure to recognize a condition that warrants a rejected landing.
Indecision.
Delay in initiating a go-around.
Failure to apply maximum allowable power in a timely manner.
Abrupt power application.
Improper pitch attitude.
Failure to configure the airplane appropriately.
Attempting to climb out of ground effect prematurely.
Failure to adequately compensate for torque/P-factor.
Loss of aircraft control.

head: Error
Fix
rows: Indecision or delay
Brief triggers before final; at the trigger, act [[24:177|AFH 9-6]] [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]
Nose rises sharply with power
Forward pressure to hold a safe attitude, then rough trim [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]
Left yaw and ball out
Right rudder for torque and P-factor [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]
All flaps up at once
Flaps partway after the descent stops, rest in small steps as you speed up [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]
Gear up before a positive rate
Gear only after a positive rate on the instruments and rough trim [[24:183|AFH 9-12]] [[24:247|AFH 12-16]]
Climb speed wandering beyond 5 knots
Set the pitch for VX or VY, trim, cross-check the airspeed; commercial band ±5 (ACS CA.IV.N.S4, S7)
Drifting off the extended centerline
Crab into the wind and recheck the ground track often [[24:140|AFH 6-8]]
Forgetting the checklist on the next approach
Re-do the entire before-landing checklist [[24:272|AFH 13-23]]

check.q: Which listed error is about leaving ground effect, and what does it cause?
check.a: Attempting to climb out of ground effect prematurely; the airplane may be unable to climb or even hold altitude at full power [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

f1.alt: An airplane descends toward a runway, then levels off low with the labels Timely decision to make go-around and Apply max power, adjust pitch attitude, and allow airspeed to increase. It then climbs: Assume climb attitude, flaps to intermediate; Positive rate of climb, retract gear, climb at VY; Retract remaining flaps; and 500 feet cruise climb.

Each box gives the throttle and elevator correction. Box 5 in the center is the desired energy state. The very slow and lower box is red and marked Dangerous: apply full throttle and avoid pitching up on the backside of the power required curve.

f3.alt: Two airplanes climb from the same runway. The steeper yellow path is labeled Best angle-of-climb airspeed (VX), greatest altitude gain in the shortest horizontal distance. The flatter red path, which ends at about the same height but farther out, is labeled Best rate-of-climb airspeed (VY), greatest altitude gain in the shortest time. Trees stand in the distance.

Labels read: Ground effect decreases induced drag; Airplane may fly at lower indicated airspeed; Accelerate in ground effect to VX or VY; Ground effect decreases quickly with height; Ground effect is negligible when height is equal to wingspan. Red arrows mark the ground effect area.

Bottom: flap deflected much more, the lift arrow moves farther aft, the pitching moment circle is larger and the tail down force arrow is much larger.

scenario.title: Hot afternoon, complex single, busy Class D
scenario.setup: You are flying a retractable-gear, constant-speed propeller single on a commercial checkride practice flight into a towered airport at 5,000 ft elevation. It is 32 C. POH: approach speed 75 KIAS, VX 72 KIAS and VY 88 KIAS at sea level, flaps up before gear unless noted. Runway 27 is in use; runway 33 crosses it about 3,500 ft from the threshold. A light jet is holding short of runway 27 at a midfield taxiway. Tower says: "Cleared to land runway 27, hold short of runway 33." Your CFI is in the right seat.

questions.q: Before you answer the tower, what must you already know to accept or decline the LAHSO clearance?
questions.a: Whether your landing distance at this density altitude fits within the published Available Landing Distance to runway 33; that check belongs in preflight planning [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]]. If not, decline; you have final authority [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]]. If you accept, read it back including 'hold short of runway 33' [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]].

questions.q: How will this field's density altitude change the go-around compared with your home field near sea level?
questions.a: Thin air cuts engine power, propeller thrust and lift [[1:91|PHAK 4-4]], so climb performance is lower [[1:264|PHAK 11-8]]. VX is higher and VY lower than the sea level numbers, so use the POH values for this altitude [[24:78|AFH 3-17]].

questions.q: At 200 ft on final, the light jet starts to taxi onto runway 27. What do you do first?
questions.a: Go around at once: power, attitude, configuration [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. A hazard appearing on the runway is a listed reason [[24:181|AFH 9-10]], and an early decision is far safer than one made close to the ground [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Then tell the tower [[24:168|AFH 8-4]].

questions.q: Where do you fly as you climb, with the jet now rolling for takeoff under you?
questions.a: Offset slightly to the side so you keep the jet in sight, flying parallel to the runway [[24:168|AFH 8-4]] [[24:272|AFH 13-23]] (ACS CA.IV.N.S6). It is a larger aircraft departing, so stay above its climb path and avoid headings that put you below and behind it [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]. Follow any tower instruction [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(b)]].

questions.q: You feel the airplane settle as your CFI asks a question and you reach for the flap handle. What should you have done, and in what order?
questions.a: Fly first: set the attitude and rough trim, and only after the descent has stopped, flaps partway in small steps; gear after a positive rate of climb [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]. A sudden flap retraction can settle the airplane [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. When overloaded, stop, think, slow down and prioritize; the question can wait [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].

questions.q: Tower clears you back to land on runway 27. What is the one item that this situation sets you up to forget?
questions.a: The gear. Re-do the entire before-landing checklist, because an interrupted habit pattern like a go-around is a classic setup for a gear-up landing [[24:272|AFH 13-23]] [[24:248|AFH 12-17]].

skills.do: Complete the right checklists, including the full before-landing checklist again before the next approach.
skills.practice: After every practice go-around, run the before-landing checklist from the top on downwind, touching each item [[24:272|AFH 13-23]] [[24:248|AFH 12-17]].

skills.do: Tell the tower you are going around (or follow its instruction), or announce your position and intentions on the CTAF.
skills.practice: Fly the airplane first, then say who you are, where you are and what you will do; ask the tower if you have no landing clearance [[24:168|AFH 8-4]] [[7:18|AC 91-73B App 3]].

skills.do: Decide on time to break off the approach when it is unstable, unsafe or outside the standards.
skills.practice: Brief your triggers on downwind and have your CFI create surprise reasons at different heights [[24:177|AFH 9-6]] [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

skills.do: Apply takeoff power at once and move to the climb attitude for VX or VY, as appropriate, holding it within 5 knots.
skills.practice: At altitude, practice full-flap, trimmed-descent go-arounds until the pitch and rudder inputs are automatic, then in the pattern [[24:126|AFH 5-21]] [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

skills.do: Configure only after a positive rate of climb is verified, or as the manufacturer says (flaps partway, then gear, then remaining flaps).
skills.practice: Say 'positive rate, gear up' only when the altimeter and VSI both show a climb, and keep your other hand on the yoke [[24:183|AFH 9-12]] [[24:247|AFH 12-16]].

skills.do: Move to the side of the runway when needed to keep conflicting traffic in sight and avoid it.
skills.practice: In practice go-arounds with traffic on the runway, offset slightly to keep it in view, then fly parallel past the departure end [[24:168|AFH 8-4]] [[24:272|AFH 13-23]] [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.6]].

skills.do: Hold VY within 5 knots up to a safe maneuvering altitude.
skills.practice: Rough trim for VY [[24:182|AFH 9-11]], then cross-check the airspeed every few seconds during the climb. Application: have your CFI call out any drift beyond 3 knots, which leaves margin inside the 5-knot band (ACS CA.IV.N.S7).

skills.do: Keep directional control and the proper wind correction so you track the extended centerline in the climb.
skills.practice: Fly go-arounds on crosswind days and check the ground track over the runway often, adjusting the crab angle [[24:140|AFH 6-8]].

skills.do: Use runway incursion avoidance procedures, such as watching the runway and hold lines on final and going around for anything on the runway.
skills.practice: Study the airport diagram before arrival and call out runway number and 'runway clear' on every final [[24:175|AFH 9-4]] [[1:365|PHAK 14-31]].

quiz.q: Which knowledge element appears in the commercial go-around Task but not in the private one?
options: Go-around procedures, timely decision, and appropriate airspeeds
Effects of wind and density altitude on a go-around or rejected landing
A stabilized approach, including energy management concepts
Wind correction techniques on takeoff, departure, approach and landing
quiz.why: CA.IV.N.K4 covers procedures, timely decision and airspeeds (ACS CA.IV.N.K4). The private Task lists only K1 to K3, which match the other three options (ACS PA.IV.N.K1 to K3).

quiz.q: The AFH and AC 61-98E both give stabilized approach criteria. On which item do they differ?
options: Bank angle on final
The 300 ft AGL point for reducing a high descent rate
The normal descent rate: AFH says generally 500 to 1,000 fpm, the AC says generally no greater than 500 fpm
Whether checklists should be done before the approach
quiz.why: AFH: generally 500 to 1,000 fpm [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. AC 61-98E: constant and generally no greater than 500 fpm [[15:12|AC 61-98E 2.1.4.5]]. Both say to reduce a rate over 500 fpm before 300 ft AGL, and both limit bank to 15 degrees and want checklists done early.

quiz.q: You are slow, low and close to the ground. Even full throttle gives no surplus power. What does the AFH say is the only recourse?
options: Pull back on the yoke to stop the sink, accepting a higher angle of attack to hold altitude
Raise the flaps at once to reduce drag, then gain speed with power
Push forward first to reduce angle of attack and drag, then gain energy with power
Hold the attitude and wait for the speed to build, then add power
quiz.why: With no excess power at full throttle, the only recourse is to trade altitude for speed by pushing forward, then add energy; near the ground there may be no room to do it [[24:99|AFH 4-13]]. Raising flaps causes a sudden loss of lift [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

quiz.q: In a constant-speed propeller airplane, what control positions give maximum takeoff power for the go-around?
options: Propeller control full forward (low pitch, high rpm), throttle to maximum allowable manifold pressure
Propeller control full aft (high pitch, low rpm) for fuel economy, throttle to maximum allowable manifold pressure
Propeller control at cruise rpm, throttle to maximum allowable manifold pressure
Throttle to maximum allowable manifold pressure first, then propeller control aft to reduce rpm
quiz.why: Maximum takeoff power: propeller control all the way forward to low pitch/high rpm and throttle to maximum allowable manifold pressure [[24:236|AFH 12-5]].

quiz.q: As an airplane climbs out of ground effect, what does the AFH say happens?
options: Less angle of attack is needed and the nose drops
More angle of attack is needed, induced drag rises, the nose tends to pitch up, and indicated airspeed increases
Induced drag falls and the airspeed reading drops
Nothing measurable above 10 ft
quiz.why: Leaving ground effect: more AOA for the same lift, more induced drag and thrust required, a pitch-up tendency, and an increase in indicated airspeed from the lower static pressure [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

quiz.q: Using the placard in Figure 12-15, what is the highest airspeed at which you may retract the gear during a go-around?
options: 129 KIAS
VY
107 KIAS
Any speed, once a positive rate is shown
quiz.why: 'GEAR UP 107 KIAS (MAX)' is the limit for operating the gear in the up direction; 129 KIAS applies to lowering it and to flying with it extended [[24:247|AFH 12-16]].

quiz.q: During a go-around in a retractable-gear airplane, why does the AFH warn about reaching for the gear selector?
options: You might select the flaps instead of the gear and cause a sudden loss of lift
Leaning forward can put forward pressure on the yoke and make the airplane descend
The gear motor needs both hands on the controls to operate the switch safely
Looking down at the selector can make you miss a radio call from the tower during the climb
quiz.why: Leaning forward to reach the gear selector may push the yoke forward and cause a descent [[24:247|AFH 12-16]].

quiz.q: Which statement about wind and the go-around climb is correct?
options: A headwind increases the rate of climb as well as the gradient over the ground, so it helps both
A crosswind improves the climb gradient because the airplane flies a longer path
Wind affects neither the rate of climb nor the climb gradient over the ground
A tailwind reduces the climb gradient over the ground but not the rate of climb
quiz.why: Rate of climb is not affected by wind; climb gradient is improved by a headwind and reduced by a tailwind [[24:259|AFH 13-10]].

quiz.q: You have no radio. On final at a towered airport you get a steady red light from the tower. What does it mean?
options: Airport unsafe, do not land, and stay clear of the airport
Return for landing, and expect a landing clearance on the next pass
Cleared to land, but watch for other traffic on the runway
Give way to other aircraft and continue circling
quiz.why: Steady red to an aircraft in flight: give way to other aircraft and continue circling. Flashing red means airport unsafe, do not land [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]].

quiz.q: What climb gradient must a newer normal category airplane show in a balked landing, with gear down and landing flaps?
options: 1.5 percent
8.3 percent
3 percent
No requirement
quiz.why: A 3 percent climb gradient, out of ground effect, with the landing gear extended and flaps in the landing configuration [[60:101|14 CFR 23.2120(c)]]. 8.3 percent is the all-engine initial climb figure for some small landplanes, in paragraph (a).

final_quiz.q: POH: VX 64 KIAS, VY 79 KIAS. You go around with a tree line just past the runway end and need the steepest climb. Which airspeed meets the commercial standard?
options: 58 KIAS
79 KIAS
71 KIAS
66 KIAS
final_quiz.why: With obstacles, VX is the appropriate speed [[24:78|AFH 3-17]]; ±5 knots gives 59 to 69 KIAS (ACS CA.IV.N.S4). 58 is too slow, 71 is out of the VX band, and 79 (VY) gives a flatter path that may not clear the trees [[1:263|PHAK 11-7]].

final_quiz.q: You fly out of a field at 6,000 ft. Compared with the sea level numbers, how do the indicated VX and VY change?
options: VX increases and VY decreases
Both decrease because the air is thinner at 6,000 ft
Both increase because the true airspeed is higher at 6,000 ft
VX decreases and VY increases as the air gets thinner
final_quiz.why: As altitude increases, the best angle of climb speed increases and the best rate of climb speed decreases, until they meet at the absolute ceiling [[24:78|AFH 3-17]].

final_quiz.q: At a non-towered airport, you go around because a slower airplane is still rolling out on the runway. Which plan best fits the sources?
options: Offset slightly to the side to keep it in sight and continue straight ahead past the departure end
Climb straight over the airplane on the centerline
Turn crosswind right away to get out of the way
Circle back on a tight base to land behind it
final_quiz.why: Consider a slight turn to offset and keep the traffic in sight [[24:272|AFH 13-23]] (ACS CA.IV.N.S6); after a go-around the upwind leg is flown parallel to the runway [[24:168|AFH 8-4]], and continue straight ahead until beyond the departure end while watching pattern traffic [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.6]].

final_quiz.q: According to the AIM, when should you decide whether you can accept a LAHSO clearance at your destination?
options: When the controller offers it, by estimating your own landing distance on the spot
During preflight planning, using the published ALD for each LAHSO combination
On short final, after seeing the hold short lights, by comparing your touchdown point to them
Only after landing, when you know your actual stopping distance on that runway
final_quiz.why: Pilots should know in advance which LAHSO combinations work for their aircraft's landing distance; good decision making is knowing ahead whether you can accept it [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]].

final_quiz.q: On an IFR flight you are cleared for a visual approach at a towered airport and must go around. Who is responsible for terrain and obstruction avoidance?
options: You, until reaching an ATC-assigned altitude if one is issued
The tower, until you reach pattern altitude, because it issues the instruction
Nobody; a visual approach has a published missed approach that provides protection
Approach control, by radar, until you are handed off again
final_quiz.why: A visual approach has no missed approach segment. The tower issues an instruction, and the pilot is responsible for terrain and obstruction avoidance until reaching an assigned altitude [[33:457|AIM 5-4-23]] [[33:458|AIM 5-4-23]].

final_quiz.q: A larger airplane takes off ahead of you just as you start a go-around on the same runway. What does the AIM recommend for your climb?
options: Stay below its flight path where the air is smooth
Hold low over the runway for 2 minutes
Follow directly in its track to keep spacing
Climb above its climb path until turning clear, and avoid headings that cross below and behind it
final_quiz.why: Departing behind a larger aircraft: continue climbing above its climb path until turning clear of its wake and avoid headings that cross below and behind it [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

final_quiz.q: You recover from a full-flap stall and hold a higher than normal climb pitch with the flaps still down. According to AC 61-67C, what may happen?
options: Nothing; flaps add lift
A secondary stall
The gear warning horn sounds
A propeller overspeed
final_quiz.why: Trying to climb with flaps extended at a higher than normal pitch can cause a secondary stall; in some airplanes even a normal climb pitch will [[13:17|AC 61-67C para 200f]].

final_quiz.q: A go-around with full flaps in a high-wing trainer. After full power, the pitch-up does not fully disappear even after the flaps are raised. Why?
options: The propeller is stuck in high pitch
Ground effect increases with height
The nose-up trim setting is still in
The ailerons are still deflected
final_quiz.why: The pitch-up tendency does not diminish completely with flap retraction because of the trim setting, so expect rapid changes in pitch forces [[24:235|AFH 12-4]].

final_quiz.q: Short final at a towered field. You never heard a landing clearance and the frequency is busy. What does the FAA's flight school guidance say to do?
options: Ask the tower if you are cleared to land, and if there is no response, go around
Land on final; the tower will call you if there is a problem, since they can see you
Rock your wings to signal the tower and continue to land
Switch to ground control and ask whether landing clearance was given
final_quiz.why: On final with no landing clearance, ask the tower; if there is no response, execute a go-around [[7:18|AC 91-73B App 3]]. Landing without clearance is a pilot deviation [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]].

final_quiz.q: Which statement about go-around accidents is supported by the sources in this lesson?
options: Most go-around accidents are caused by engine failures
Go-arounds have no accident history in GA
Many power-on stall/spin accidents have happened during go-arounds, linked to nose-high trim and premature flap retraction
Go-around accidents happen mostly above 1,000 ft AGL
final_quiz.why: AC 61-67C says many power-on stall/spin accidents occurred during go-arounds, with nose-high trim and premature flap retraction as causal factors [[13:11|AC 61-67C para 104]]. The sources give no percentages for go-around accidents.

final_quiz.q: You are on a hot, gusty day, 600 ft AGL on final, and the airspeed suddenly drops 15 knots with a strong sink and virga ahead. What is the best action?
options: Lower the nose to regain the lost airspeed, then continue the approach and land if the airspeed recovers
Extend full flaps for more lift and keep the approach speed constant
Reduce power to avoid ballooning in the sink and hold the same pitch attitude
Go around now, and in the climb do not let pitch fall below the normal range, accepting lower airspeed
final_quiz.why: Be ready to go around at the first sign of a microburst [[28:266|AWH 22-11]]. To protect the flight path, do not let pitch fall below the normal range and accept reduced airspeed [[28:268|AWH 22-13]].

final_quiz.q: Climbing out after a go-around in a gusty crosswind, why should you recheck your ground track several times?
options: Because VY changes every 100 ft of climb and needs a new pitch setting
Because the heading indicator precesses during climbs and must be reset to the compass often
Because ATC requires a ground track report during every go-around climb
Because the crosswind can change markedly within a few hundred feet of the ground
final_quiz.why: The force of a crosswind may vary markedly within a few hundred feet of the ground, so check the ground track often and adjust the wind correction angle [[24:140|AFH 6-8]] (ACS CA.IV.N.S8).

final_quiz.q: The PHAK names three major causal areas for runway incursions. Which is one of them?
options: Engine failure on takeoff because of poor maintenance
Failure to comply with ATC instructions
Night operations only, when visual cues are limited
Wake turbulence from a preceding departing airplane
final_quiz.why: The three areas are failure to comply with ATC instructions, lack of airport familiarity and nonconformance with standard operating procedures [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]].

takeaways: A go-around is normal; it only kills when it is late or sloppy. Beat landing expectancy and pride with triggers briefed before final.
Stabilized by 500 ft above the airport in VMC; unstable below 300 ft AGL in the pattern means go around now.
Power, attitude, configuration: full power smoothly, forward pressure and right rudder, rough trim, then flaps partway, gear after a positive rate, rest of the flaps.
Commercial band: VX or VY ±5 knots, then VY ±5 knots to a safe maneuvering altitude.
Ground effect is borrowed performance; do not climb out of it too soon, and expect a pitch-up and odd instrument readings.
High density altitude, weight, gear and flaps cut climb; a tailwind flattens the climb gradient.
Offset to keep traffic in sight, stay above a larger aircraft's path, tell ATC or the CTAF, and re-run the whole before-landing checklist.
cfi_notes: The only skill changes from private are the climb-speed bands: ±5 knots instead of +10/-5 in S4 and S7 (ACS CA.IV.N.S4, S7; PA.IV.N.S4, S7). K4 is new at the commercial level, so expect oral questions on procedure, timing and airspeeds (ACS CA.IV.N.K4).

The sources disagree on the normal stabilized descent rate: the AFH says generally 500 to 1,000 fpm [[24:177|AFH 9-6]], the newer AC 61-98E says generally no greater than 500 fpm [[15:12|AC 61-98E 2.1.4.5]]. Both say a rate above 500 fpm should be reduced before 300 ft AGL. Teach the 300 ft rule as the hard line.

The single-engine sources only say the upwind leg after a go-around is flown parallel to the runway [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]; the explicit 'slight turn to offset' for traffic is in the AFH twin-engine chapter [[24:272|AFH 13-23]], though nothing in it depends on two engines. AC 90-66C says go-arounds continue straight ahead until past the departure end [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.6]], the P/CG says a VFR go-around at a towered field overflies the runway unless ATC says otherwise [[34:353|AIM P/CG]], and AIM 4-3-12 says a planned low approach makes no turns until a visual check [[33:256|AIM 4-3-12]]. Teach them together: a small offset to keep traffic in view, then parallel and straight ahead, and ATC instructions first.

Figure 9-12 shows a twin turboprop and a '500 feet cruise climb'. Point out that the sequence is the same for a single and that 500 ft is an example, not a rule; the ACS just says 'safe maneuvering altitude'.

The AFH gives two slightly different ground effect numbers: about 50 percent less induced drag at one-tenth span [[24:142|AFH 6-10]] versus 47.6 percent in the PHAK [[1:108|PHAK 5-11]]. Same idea; do not let students get stuck on it.

Demonstrate the elevator trim stall at altitude before the student flies go-arounds in the pattern; AC 61-67C's go-around demo lets the nose rise and the airplane swerve left on purpose so the student feels it [[13:18|AC 61-67C para 200g]].

Call go-arounds from every phase, including the round out at low speed and after a bounce. Teach the 'few moments of level flight to accelerate' idea [[24:272|AFH 13-23]] so students do not pitch for VY with no airspeed.

In complex airplanes, watch for the student grabbing the gear handle early. Make 'positive rate' mean both the altimeter and the VSI, since ground effect can make the VSI read oddly near the runway [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

Accident data in these sources is qualitative for go-arounds (AC 61-67C 'many stall/spin accidents') [[13:11|AC 61-67C para 104]]; the only hard numbers are for runway incursions [[1:365|PHAK 14-31]] [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]]. Do not quote go-around accident percentages to students without a source.
gaps: Airplane-specific items come from the AFM/POH: go-around power settings, propeller and mixture settings for the approach and go-around, flap retraction steps, VX and VY at altitude, and gear operating speeds. The sources give no mixture guidance for a high density altitude go-around.
Neither the ACS nor these sources define 'safe maneuvering altitude' for S7. Figure 9-12 shows 500 ft as an example only. Agree on a number with your CFI and examiner.
No standard CTAF phraseology for a VFR go-around is given; AC 90-66C only shows a sample call for breaking off an instrument approach [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.4.3]].
The sources give no statistics on how many accidents involve go-arounds, only that many power-on stall/spin accidents happen during them [[13:11|AC 61-67C para 104]].

The only source that names a sideways offset for traffic is the AFH twin-engine chapter; the single-engine pattern chapter only says the upwind leg after a go-around is flown parallel to the runway. No source says how far to offset. The wind shear encounter guidance in the AWH comes from airline studies, and there is no small-airplane wind shear escape procedure in these sources.

The 3 percent balked landing gradient is from the current Part 23 [[60:101|14 CFR 23.2120(c)]]. Most training airplanes were certified under older rules that these sources do not include, so check the AFM/POH for what your airplane actually shows.

activities.title: Find the energy state on the chart
activities.intro: Drag each situation to the box of the energy chart that describes it. Think about whether you are high or low, and fast or slow.

pins.label: 150 ft above the glide path and 8 knots slow
High and fast at 600 ft AGL
On the glide path but 10 knots fast
Below the glide path, right on target speed
Below the glide path and 10 knots fast
Low, stall horn sounding, sinking toward the trees

activities.why: Rows are altitude (higher, desired, lower) and columns are airspeed (very slow, slower, desired, faster). Each situation sits where its row and column meet [[24:99|AFH 4-13]]. The low and very slow box is the dangerous one: full throttle and do not pitch up [[24:99|AFH 4-13]].

activities.title: Go-around decision points, from downwind to touchdown
activities.intro: Put the decision points in the order you meet them on a VFR pattern in a retractable-gear airplane. Use the arrows, then tap Check.
steps: Downwind, opposite the landing point: gear down and before-landing checklist done
Turn to final: if it would create a collision hazard with traffic on final, go around
500 ft above airport elevation: not stabilized, go around
Passing 300 ft AGL: any descent rate above 500 fpm already reduced
Below 300 ft AGL: approach becomes unstabilized, go around immediately
Round out: cannot land in the first third of the runway, go around
Touchdown: severe bounce, go around at once
activities.why: Gear by the point opposite the landing spot [[24:248|AFH 12-17]]; base-to-final conflict [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]; 500 ft and 300 ft gates [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]; first third [[24:203|AFH 9-32]]; severe bounce [[24:205|AFH 9-34]].

activities.title: True or false: climbing out of the go-around
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: In ground effect right after liftoff, the VSI usually shows a descent.
cards.why: True. Higher local static pressure in ground effect makes the airspeed and altimeter read slightly low and usually makes the VSI show a descent [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

cards.s: At a height of one-quarter wingspan, induced drag is reduced by about 25 percent.
cards.why: True. About 25 percent at one-quarter span, and about 50 percent at one-tenth span [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

cards.s: VX is usually slightly faster than VY.
cards.why: False. VX is usually slightly less than VY [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

cards.s: Unless the AFM/POH says otherwise, the flaps come up at least partly before the gear is retracted in a go-around.
cards.why: True. On most airplanes full flaps make more drag than the gear, and if the airplane touches down early you want the gear still down and locked [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

cards.s: Maximum rate of climb at VY always clears an obstacle that VX would clear.
cards.why: False. Maximum rate of climb may not be enough to avoid an obstacle that maximum angle of climb would clear [[1:263|PHAK 11-7]].

cards.s: If you are slow when you start the go-around, it may be right to lower the nose briefly to gain airspeed.
cards.why: True. Resist pitching up without airspeed; lowering the nose briefly keeps you off the back side of the power curve [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

activities.title: More climb, or less climb?
activities.intro: Tap a change, then tap where it belongs.

items.t: Retracting the landing gear after a positive rate
Moving flaps from full to the takeoff setting
Leaving the gear down well into the climb
Lighter load after burning off fuel
A hot, humid afternoon at a high field

activities.why: More weight, more altitude, gear down or flaps down all reduce excess thrust and power, so climb drops; less weight helps [[1:264|PHAK 11-8]]. Full flaps make more drag than the gear [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]. High, hot and humid raise density altitude and cut power, thrust and lift; cold, dry, high pressure lowers it [[1:91|PHAK 4-4]].

activities.title: Go-around climb numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer. For gradients, 1 knot of groundspeed is about 101.3 ft per minute (6,076 ft per NM divided by 60).

items.q: POH VX is 62 KIAS. You go around with trees ahead and use VX. What is the lowest airspeed that still meets the commercial standard?
Calm wind, groundspeed 70 knots, rate of climb 650 fpm. What is the climb gradient?
items.why: Horizontal travel: 70 x 101.27 = 7,089 ft per minute. Gradient = 650 / 7,089 x 100 = 9.2 percent. Climb gradient is altitude gained per 100 ft of horizontal travel [[24:251|AFH 13-2]].

items.q: Same airspeed and 650 fpm, but now into a 15-knot headwind (groundspeed 55 knots). What is the climb gradient?
items.why: 55 x 101.27 = 5,570 ft per minute. 650 / 5,570 x 100 = 11.7 percent. A headwind improves the gradient; the rate of climb is unchanged [[24:259|AFH 13-10]].

items.q: Same again with a 10-knot tailwind (groundspeed 80 knots). What is the climb gradient?
items.why: 80 x 101.27 = 8,101 ft per minute. 650 / 8,101 x 100 = 8.0 percent. A tailwind reduces the gradient [[24:259|AFH 13-10]].

items.q: 14 CFR 23.2120(c) requires a 3 percent balked landing climb gradient (out of ground effect, gear down, landing flaps). In calm wind at 65 knots true airspeed (groundspeed 65 knots), what rate of climb is that, to the nearest 10 fpm?
items.why: 65 x 101.27 = 6,582 ft per minute of travel. 3 percent of that: 0.03 x 6,582 = 197 fpm, about 200 fpm [[60:101|14 CFR 23.2120(c)]].

items.q: At an 8 percent climb gradient, how much height do you gain over 3,000 ft of runway?
items.why: 8 ft per 100 ft x 30 = 240 ft. Gradient is altitude per 100 ft of horizontal travel [[24:251|AFH 13-2]].

activities.title: Where and how: go-around rules by situation
activities.intro: Tap a situation, then the rule the sources give for it.

pairs.l: Planned low approach in a Class D surface area
pairs.r: Ask the tower for approval before starting final

pairs.l: Tower says 'go around' to a VFR airplane and adds nothing
pairs.r: Overfly the runway climbing to pattern altitude, enter on the crosswind leg

pairs.l: Overshooting the turn from base to final, low
pairs.r: Go around; no steep bank and no skidding turn

pairs.l: Traffic on the runway may not clear in time
pairs.r: Go around early and inform the controller
Keep safe separation and notify the controller promptly
Move the throttle smoothly and watch for overboost

activities.why: Low approach [[33:256|AIM 4-3-12]]; ATC 'go around' [[34:353|AIM P/CG]]; base-to-final overshoot [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]; traffic on the runway [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]; LAHSO [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]]; turbocharger [[24:241|AFH 12-10]].

activities.title: Truck on the runway, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are flying N731CP, a retractable-gear, constant-speed propeller single, with your CFI on a commercial training flight. Non-towered airport, 4,000 ft runway, wind calm. POH: flaps up in steps, gear up after a positive rate, VY 84 KIAS. You are on short final at 150 ft AGL, full flaps, gear down, trimmed for 75 KIAS.

steps.s: A fuel truck drives onto the runway at the first taxiway, 800 ft ahead of your aiming point.
options: Continue and plan to land beyond the truck once it has left the runway
Slow down and S-turn to give it time to clear the runway
Go around now: full power, attitude, configuration
Add 10 knots and fly over it to land long on the remaining runway
steps.why: An unexpected hazard on the runway is a reason to go around [[24:181|AFH 9-10]], and the decision should be immediate; the go-around becomes dangerous when delayed [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. S-turns at 150 ft are exactly the low-altitude maneuvering risk the ACS lists (ACS CA.IV.N.R6).

steps.s: You push the throttle and propeller forward smoothly. The nose rises sharply and the airplane yaws left.
options: Let it rise; you need altitude and the trim will sort itself out
Forward pressure to hold a safe attitude, right rudder, then rough trim
Raise the flaps right away to reduce the pitch-up, then add forward pressure later
Pull power back until the nose settles and the yaw stops
steps.why: Full power with nose-up trim raises the nose and yaws left; use considerable forward pressure, right rudder for torque and P-factor, then rough trim [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Nose-high trim and early flap retraction are causal factors in go-around stall accidents [[13:11|AC 61-67C para 104]].

steps.s: The descent has stopped at 120 ft. Airspeed 76 KIAS and increasing. The VSI is still near zero.
options: Gear up now, since the descent has stopped and you are at full power
All flaps up now, since the descent has stopped and the airspeed is rising
Leave everything as it is until pattern altitude, then clean up
Flaps partway (takeoff or intermediate setting), gear stays down
steps.why: After the descent has stopped, move the flaps partway or to the takeoff setting, in small steps [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. The gear stays down until a positive rate of climb, in case of an accidental touchdown [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]. Leaving full flaps is a high-drag go-around [[24:103|AFH 4-17]].

steps.s: Now the altimeter and VSI both show a climb, rough trim is done, and you are passing the truck, offset just to the side so you can see it.
options: Gear up, then the rest of the flaps in steps as you accelerate to VY
Raise all the flaps at once, then the gear, to clean up the drag quickly
Hold everything as is until 1,000 ft AGL, then clean up
Turn crosswind now to clear the runway for the traffic behind
steps.why: With a positive rate and rough trim done, retract the gear, then the remaining flaps in small steps [[24:183|AFH 9-12]] [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. At a non-towered airport, continue straight ahead until beyond the departure end [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.6]].

steps.s: At pattern altitude on downwind, the truck is off the runway. Your CFI says 'Same landing again.'
options: Announce on the CTAF and run the entire before-landing checklist, gear down by the point opposite the landing spot
Flaps down and land; the gear is already handled
Skip the radio call; you just made one
Fly a straight-in to save time
steps.why: After a go-around, re-accomplish the entire before-landing checklist; an interrupted habit pattern is a classic setup for a gear-up landing [[24:272|AFH 13-23]]. The gear goes down by the point opposite the landing spot on downwind [[24:248|AFH 12-17]].
